nomenclature.en: Extraocular Muscle Fibre Fine Structure and Classification

content.definition: The fine structure and classification of extraocular muscle fibres. Extraocular muscles contain both twitch (singly innervated, 'fibrillenstruktur') and tonic (multiply innervated, 'felderstruktur') fibres that do not correspond to the skeletal muscle types I, IIA, IIB and IIC, because ocular muscle fibres contain specific myosins different from those of limb muscle (p.119). The Spencer and Porter (1981) numeric nomenclature recognises six fibre types: two in the orbital zone (types 1-2) and four in the global zone (types 3-6) (Tables 4.4, 4.5, pp.119-121).
content.location: The fibre types are compartmentalised into the orbital zone (types 1-2) and the global zone (types 3-6) of each extraocular muscle (pp.119-121). The levator muscle is not divided into orbital and global zones (p.124). The section applies to all six extraocular muscles; fibre diameters are given in Table 4.3 and the change in fibre diameter with age was reported by Engel and Brooke (1966) (p.122).
layers: Why ocular fibres do not fit skeletal nomenclature: skeletal terminology based on histochemistry refers only to singly innervated twitch fibres and cannot completely describe extraocular subtypes which also include tonic fibres (Asmussen et al. 1971; Spencer and Porter 1981; Porter et al. 1995) (p.119). Histochemically type II fibres appear singly innervated with single motor end plates, while at least some type I (slow twitch) fibres show a multiple pattern of innervation — a characteristic of tonic fibres (p.119).

Type 1 — orbital singly innervated (fast twitch): small fibres making up 80% of the orbital layer, probably accounting for most of the sustained force generated by the muscle. Mitochondria occur in abundant clusters and individual fibres are ringed by capillaries. Coarse fast-twitch fibres rich in oxidative enzymes but also capable of anaerobic metabolism, corresponding to skeletal type II; myosin isoforms vary along the fibre — a fast myosin in the mid-portion, and generic fast myosin, IIA, embryonic/neonatal myosin and an eye-muscle-specific myosin away from the mid-zone (Jacoby, Chiarandini and Stefani 1989). High fatigue resistance and unique myosin profile distinguish it from skeletal IIA. Its elaborate motor end plates literally encircle the fibre and may have been confused with spiral sensory endings (Ruskell and Wilson 1983) (pp.119-120).

Type 2 — orbital multiply innervated (tonic): a slow fibre resembling 'amphibian tonic' fibres, 20% of the orbital zone. Stains strongly for myosin ATPase after acid preincubation, variably with alkaline ATPase; acid-stable myosin ATPase found only in the proximal and distal thirds. Sparse membranous systems, irregular myofibrillar arrangement. Centrally resembles skeletal fast twitch (IIC) with a fast myosin isoform, while at either end it shows the ultrastructure and slow ATPase of slow contracting fibres and contains an embryonic/neonatal myosin. Twitch capability near the centre with slow contractility proximally and distally (Jacoby 1989; Davidowitz 1980; 1982) (p.120).

Type 3 — global red singly innervated: makes up 30% of the global layer. Stains coarsely and resembles the orbital singly innervated fibre; highly oxidative and glycolytic, regarded as fatigue resistant. No longitudinal structural variation; expresses myosin IIA along its length but differs from skeletal IIA by its high mitochondrial content (Bruckner et al. 1994); assumed fast-twitch and fatigue resistant (p.120).

Type 4 — global intermediate singly innervated: 25% of the global layer. Ultrastructure and ATPase content suggest a fast-twitch fibre; myosin reactivity suggests resemblance to a skeletal fast fibre subtype (Bruckner et al. 1994). Histologically granular with moderate levels of oxidative and aerobic enzymes; numerous small mitochondria singly or in clusters; myofibril size and sarcoplasmic reticulum content intermediate between the other two singly innervated fibres (p.120).

Type 5 — global pale singly innervated: comprises 30% of the global layer. Resembles skeletal IIB: modest levels of oxidative enzymes, high anaerobic metabolic capacity, fast-type myosin ATPase. Acetylcholine staining shows the single locus of large end plates. Mitochondria small and few, arranged singly between myofibrils. Overall profile of a fast twitch fibre used infrequently because of low fatigue resistance. Fibre diameter increases from types 3 to 5 (pp.120-121).
Types 3-5 share a regular myofibrillar arrangement on electron microscopy with well-developed sarcoplasmic reticulum and T systems (slightly less in type 5); all are singly innervated (p.121).

Type 6 — global multiply innervated (tonic): a slow fibre resembling 'amphibian tonic', 10% of the global layer. Strong acid-stable ATPase features, weak oxidative properties. Felderstruktur with very large myofibrils, sparse membranous systems and occasional mitochondria in single file. Multiply innervated with numerous en grappe endings along its length; unlike type 2, staining is homogeneous. Myosin expression includes slow-twitch (type I), slow tonic and (in the rabbit) alpha cardiac myosin (Pierobon-Bormioli et al. 1979, 1980; Jacoby et al. 1990; Roll et al. 1990) (p.121).

Myosin isoforms: as many as ten heavy myosin isoforms, each with different contractile properties and encoded by distinct mammalian genes (Storm and Johnson 1993). A clearer picture of the specificity and diversity of extraocular subtypes has emerged from immunohistochemical studies (Bormioli 1980; Rowlerson 1987; Sartore 1987; Jacoby 1989, 1990; Moll 1990; Porter 1995) (p.121). The Rowlerson (1987) classification (Table 4.6) recognises immature twitch, orbital tonic and slow twitch, and global slow twitch plus extraocular-specific fast twitch fibres (pp.121-122).

The vertebrate extraocular muscle myosin is distinct from skeletal muscle myosins — no cross-reaction — which may explain the differences in twitch contraction times and the very low specific tension output (maximum isometric tetanic tension per unit cross-sectional area) of extraocular muscle: rat inferior rectus is about one-third to one-half the value for rat limb muscle (pp.121-122).

Immature myosins: many orbital fibres coexpress embryonic or neonatal myosins with the specific 'fast' extraocular myosin; the proportion declines with age but does not disappear entirely (Wieczorek et al. 1985). The persistence of immature myosins may relate to the limited load bearing of extraocular muscles (Sartore et al. 1987). Postnatal maturation of the extraocular muscles parallels maturation of retinal circuitry and establishment of interocular alignment; the most significant development is the increase in mitochondrial content — development of eye movements parallels the acquisition of fatigue resistance (p.121).

Antibody-defined slow fibres: antibodies against 'slow fibre' myosins identify two further ocular fibre types, a slow-twitch and a tonic fibre, with a (skeletal) type I histochemical profile; the tonic fibre corresponds to Asmussen's multiply innervated type 2; the two are distinguished by an antibody specific for vertebrate tonic fibres (Rowlerson 1987) (pp.121-122).

Stimulation and contraction of twitch fibres: acetylcholine stored in the axon terminal is released across the synaptic cleft, a 40-50 nm gap, binding to receptors on the crests of the postjunctional sarcolemmal folds. The resting potential of the muscle fibre is about -65 to -90 mV and depolarisation occurs when the potential reaches -60 to -55 mV; spontaneous quantal release produces the miniature end-plate potential (mepp) and contraction is initiated by the end-plate potential (epp), which generates a propagated muscle action potential conducted to the sarcoplasmic reticulum via the T system, releasing calcium (Ridgway and Gordon 1975). Excitation-contraction coupling: calcium binding to troponin exposes myosin binding sites on actin; cross-bridge cycling slides thin over thick filaments, powered by ATP hydrolysis by myosin ATPase in the globular (HMM) heads; the twitch is terminated by Ca2+-dependent ATPase pumps restoring free calcium (pp.125-126).

Extraocular twitch contraction is the fastest in the body: 7.5-10 ms for medial rectus compared with 40 ms for gastrocnemius. The stimulation frequency to induce fusion of extraocular responses is 350-450 Hz (Lennerstrand 1986) compared with 100 Hz for gastrocnemius; the fusion frequency for extraocular muscle is about ten times that required to induce the twitch responses (Cooper and Eccles 1930; Bach-y-Rita and Ito 1966; Lennerstrand 1974), for skeletal muscle the ratio is about two times greater. Increasing stimulation above 350 Hz increases the rate of rise of tension but not the level achieved (Barmack et al. 1971; Fuchs and Luschei 1971) (p.126).

Tonic fibre contraction: stimulation of multiply innervated fibres produces a slowly graded contraction (Hofmann and Lembeck 1969; Eakins and Katz 1971); fusion frequency is 200 Hz or lower, and stimulation at up to 400 Hz increases the force but neither rate nor force increases above this. Tonic fibres do not exhibit a propagated action potential — a passive electrotonic spread of depolarisation from multiple sites; the miniature small nerve junctional potentials are smaller than end-plate potentials; the resting potential is lower and membrane resistance about six times greater than in twitch fibres (p.129).

Acetylcholine receptor isoforms: two developmentally regulated isoforms with five subunits — embryonic alpha2-beta-gamma-delta and adult alpha2-beta-epsilon. The embryonic isoform is thought to be retained by multiply innervated fibres. The advanced and sometimes exclusive involvement of extraocular muscles in myasthenia gravis has been attributed to differences in the acetylcholine receptor types expressed in extraocular versus skeletal muscle (Horton et al. 1993; Oda 1993) (p.126).

Pharmacology: succinylcholine, a depolarising blocker in skeletal muscle, selectively activates multiply innervated extraocular fibres (certainly global, possibly orbital), so ocular alignment under general anaesthesia approximates the primary position. The aminoacyl local anaesthetics (lidocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine) are myotoxic — they induce calcium release from intracellular stores and sarcolemmal disruption — so unanticipated ptosis or diplopia may follow ocular surgery under local anaesthesia; in the monkey the severe response occurs only in the global, pale singly innervated fibres. Botulinum toxin A blocks the calcium-dependent release of acetylcholine (Cull-Candy 1976) and is used clinically for transient weakening of extraocular muscles in squint management (Scott 1973, 1980); in extraocular muscles there are permanent effects — in the monkey a specific loss of orbital singly innervated muscle (Spencer and McNeer 1987), more profound in infantile and juvenile animals (McNeer 1991; Spencer 1992) (pp.129-130).

Normal 'myopathic' features: normal human extraocular muscle commonly shows changes that in skeletal muscle would be read as myopathic or degenerative — whorled fibres, vacuoles within myofibrillar bundles, hypolemmal inclusions, sarcomere disruption, nemaline rods, smeared Z-lines, mitochondrial clumping, Zebra and Hirano bodies (Martinez et al. 1976), and 'Ringbinden' fibres; plus variability in fibre shape and size, a higher proportion of smaller fibres, more nuclei and a mild mononuclear infiltrate (Ringel et al. 1978). The reason is obscure and may hinder interpretation of biopsies (p.129).

Ageing: extraocular muscle shows signs of ageing from early adult life, with a differential loss of type II fibres (IIa according to Lyness 1986) from the orbital and then the global layer and a later loss of global 'type I' fibres (Lyness 1986); mean fibre width of all types is maintained with age but the variance increases (p.129).

Functional correlates: the singly innervated, fast, oxidative orbital fibres show the greatest phylogenetic differences and are particularly well developed in primates — an adaptation related to binocular fusional requirements and the emergence of vergence and smooth pursuit subsystems (Walls 1962); a potential role may be maintaining stability of fixation over a wide range of gaze. The global multiply innervated fibres associated with palisade endings at the myotendinous junction may contribute a significant part of the holding tension in the primary position and may smooth and dampen antagonistic muscles during fixation (Browne 1976) (p.129).
content.blood_supply: Type 1 (orbital singly innervated) fibres are individually ringed by capillaries (p.119); overall, the extraocular muscles have a blood flow, and hence potential oxidative capacity, higher than in any skeletal muscle (p.156).
content.innervation: Twitch fibres are innervated by branches of single motor axons terminating as 'en plaque' motor end plates rich in cholinesterase, distributed over a region 1-2 mm wide in the middle third of the belly, just distal to the union of nerve trunk and muscle (Dietert 1965). The levator is innervated entirely with en plaque endings, as is about 85% of human extraocular muscle (p.124). There is a bimodal distribution of axonal diameters in the ocular motor nerves, with peaks at 5 and 11 um; the larger axons innervate twitch fibres and the smaller, tonic fibres; there is evidence for limited division of motor axons after exit from the brain stem — Bars (1926) found an 11% increase in axons of the third and fourth nerves at entry into the muscle, and Torre (1953) similar findings for the sixth nerve (pp.124-125). Tonic fibres are innervated by multiple 'en grappe' endings (Kupfer 1960; Hess 1961; Bormioli 1980), concentrated over the distal third of the belly (Cheng 1963; Dietert 1965); many endings occur on a single fibre, with clusters separated by 10 um to 2-3 mm; although each en grappe ending is much smaller than a motor end plate, the total junctional area offered is probably 12-48% greater; the supplying axons are of smaller calibre (pp.128-129). Zone proportions (Table 4.8, all percentages): human child 86% single/14% multiple (Muhlendyk 1978); human adult 80-90%/10-20% (Namba et al. 1968); human adult orbital 8%/92% and global 67%/33% (Ringel et al. 1978); monkey 85%/15% (Mayr 1966); baboon orbital 20%/80%, global 88%/12% (Durston 1974); cat 70%/30% (Alvarado and Van Horn 1975); sheep 84%/16% (Harker 1972); rat 86%/14% (Mayr 1971) (p.124).
content.histology_summary: Two fibre systems distinguish extraocular from skeletal muscle: twitch fibres with fibrillenstruktur (regular myofibrils, well-developed sarcoplasmic reticulum and T systems, single en plaque end plates) and tonic fibres with felderstruktur (irregular myofibrils, sparse membranous systems, multiple en grappe endings). Spencer and Porter (1981) six-type scheme: orbital zone 80% type 1 (singly innervated fast) and 20% type 2 (multiply innervated tonic); global zone 30% type 3 (red SI), 25% type 4 (intermediate SI), 30% type 5 (pale SI) and 10% type 6 (multiply innervated tonic). Ocular fibres carry specific myosins (up to ten heavy isoforms), including an extraocular-specific fast myosin, which explains their exceptionally fast contraction and very low specific tension output (pp.119-122).
content.clinical_importance: The unique fibre biology explains documented clinical phenomena: the fastest contraction of any muscle (7.5-10 ms medial rectus) with a fusion frequency of 350-450 Hz (p.126); the advanced and sometimes exclusive involvement of extraocular muscle in myasthenia gravis, attributed to acetylcholine receptor isoform differences (Horton et al. 1993; Oda 1993, p.126); unanticipated ptosis or diplopia after ocular surgery under local anaesthesia from the myotoxicity of aminoacyl anaesthetics (p.129); the aligning effect of succinylcholine under general anaesthesia (p.129); botulinum toxin A for transient strabismus management, with documented permanent loss of orbital singly innervated fibres in monkeys (p.130); the normal 'myopathic-looking' changes that complicate biopsy interpretation (p.129); and the differential age-related loss of type II fibres (Lyness 1986, p.129).
